name: Kanakagiri Jain Tirth
significance: A Jain pilgrimage centre near Maleyuru whose rock-cut and structural shrines begin with a Parshvanatha temple raised under the Western Gangas. Inscriptions spanning Ganga, Hoysala, Vijayanagara and Wadiyar patronage mark it as a long-lived monastic and institutional seat of Karnataka Jainism.
story: Local tradition holds that Mahavira himself came here and held a samavasarana assembly, and that a Mysore queen was freed of kalasarpadosha through worship at the site.

name: Varahanatha Temple
deity: Varaha (Shveta Varaha, boar avatar of Vishnu)
significance: An ASI-protected temple on the island formed by the Vaitarani at Jajpur, enshrining the white Varaha form of Vishnu; the Madala Panji credits its building to Prataparudra Deva and it was later renovated under the Maratha ruler Raghoji I Bhonsle. Its deula and cluster of subsidiary shrines are a substantial example of medieval Kalinga temple building.
story: Legend says that when the Vedas were stolen during Brahma's ashvamedha sacrifice here, Vishnu rose from the sacrificial fire as the boar Varaha to recover them.

name: Jatileswar Temple
significance: An early Shiva shrine in the Jalpaiguri plains dated to the Gupta period and attributed to a feudatory of the Gupta kingdom. It is protected as an archaeological site and a West Bengal State Protected Monument, making it one of north Bengal's oldest surviving temple remains.

name: Vayalil Thrikkovil Mahavishnu Temple
significance: A Vishnu shrine in Kollam district historically owned by the Pisharikkal Mana of Kodungallur and now run by a local temple forum. It remains an active worship centre known for its fortnightly Lakshmi Narayana pooja and the Ashtami Rohini festival.

name: Arang Jain Temples
significance: A group of Jain temples at Arang, of which the late 11th-century Bhand Dewal is the principal survivor, built under the Haihaya rulers of the region. Their sculpted tirthankara images and brick and stone detailing record Arang's standing as a joint Jain and Hindu religious centre in medieval Chhattisgarh.

name: Varadaraja Perumal Temple, Poonamallee
significance: A Vishnu temple in the Chennai suburb of Poonamallee, reckoned about a thousand years old and associated with the Vaishnava acharya Thirukatchi Nambi. Its Chola-period tank of over an acre long watered the surrounding paddy fields and supplied the town with domestic water.

name: Raidongia Doul
significance: An Ahom-period doul begun in 1742 under Swargadeo Pramatta Singha and completed in the late 1750s, originally a Devi temple and now dedicated to Shiva; it was granted to the Raidongia king on his marriage to the king's sister Yamini. Assam's archaeology department lists it as a State Protected Monument for its Ahom sculptural work depicting Hindu deities and avatars.

name: Veetrirundha Perumal Temple
builtDisplay: rebuilt in stone c. 850 (Pallava); brick original c. 400
significance: One of only two surviving pre-Pallava temple sites in Tamil Nadu, begun as a brick shrine and rebuilt in stone around 850 CE under Nandivarman II. Later renovations by Rajaraja Chola and by Krishnadevaraya in 1520 make it a compact record of successive South Indian building phases.
story: The name, meaning the seated lord, is explained by the tradition that Rama sat here in grief and was comforted by Bhumi Devi and Nila Devi fanning him with a palm leaf.

name: Gingee Venkataramana Temple
significance: The largest temple at the fort town of Gingee, raised around 1540-1550 by Muthyala Nayaka in full Vijayanagara idiom. Its ornamental pillars were dismantled by the French garrison in 1761 and further sculpture was carried off in 1860, so the ruin also documents the colonial dispersal of South Indian temple fabric.

name: Beeramgunta Poleramma Temple
significance: A village shrine in Nellore district dedicated to Poleramma, a pre-Vedic guardian goddess widely worshipped as a local form of Shakti across Andhra Pradesh. First put up by a British-era village officer roughly two centuries ago, it was later rebuilt with funds raised by the villagers themselves and remains a working centre of folk-deity worship and annual festivals.

name: Baneswar Shiva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple about ten kilometres from Cooch Behar town whose linga stands in an underground sanctum beneath a squarish domed structure with a curved cornice. Its foundation is contested between several traditions, variously crediting Raja Jalpeswar, the Khen ruler Nilambar, and the Koch rulers Nara Narayan and Pran Narayan, and it draws large crowds at Maha Shivaratri.
story: Tradition tells that the demon king Banasura persuaded Shiva to come down to earth, and that when Banasura halted at Baneswar the god vanished, leaving a linga on the bank of the Bangti river.

name: Mahudi Jain Temple
deity: Padmaprabha (complex also centred on Ghantakarna Mahavir)
significance: A Shvetambara Jain pilgrimage complex founded by the monk Buddhisagarsuri, its foundation stone laid in 1916 and the temple established the following year. Scholars credit it with turning the worship of the protective deity Ghantakarna Mahavir from a largely private monastic transmission into a public devotional cult that now draws well beyond the Jain community.

name: Adhirangam Ranganathaswamy Temple
significance: A five-acre Vishnu temple built up by Chola and Vijayanagara patrons, holding a reclining image some 29 feet long and counted among the 108 Abhimana Kshetrams of Vaishnavism. It is reputed to be older than Srirangam, which gives it the name Adhi Rangam, and it preserves an unusual brick grain store.
story: The temple's legend has Ranganatha rise from the water here to recover the Vedas stolen by the demon king Somukan and to counsel Brahma.

name: Kamteswari Temple
significance: A goddess temple at Gosanimari raised in 1665 by Maharaja Pran Narayan of Cooch Behar to replace an earlier shrine that had been destroyed. Standing 14 metres high on a square base with a curved cornice and circular dome, it is a state-protected monument and holds Pala-era sculpture alongside its images.

name: Bezor Doul
significance: A late-medieval brick temple with an octagonal sanctuary, built under the Ahom king Rudra Singha in memory of a Bezbarua, a court physician granted extensive land in the area for his skill in traditional medicine. Though it holds no images inside, it remains in worship and is a State Protected Monument of Assam.

name: Vijayanarayana Temple, Gundlupet
significance: A Vishnu temple in Gundlupet town going back to 10th-century Western Ganga rule, with patronage continuing into the Vijayanagara period. Its yali-pillared entrance, Garuda and Hanuman sculpture, and garbhagriha-navaranga-mandapa plan make it a working example of medieval South Indian temple craft.
story: Tradition credits the Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana with consecrating the image of Vijayanarayana here.

name: Murali Mohan Temple
significance: A Krishna temple at Bishnupur built in 1665 by Churamoni Devi, wife of the Mallabhum king Bir Singha Dev. Its single tower over a pillared covered ambulatory is a textbook example of the Bengal ek-ratna form, and the ASI holds it as a Monument of National Importance.

name: Surya Temple, Ranchi
significance: A modern sun temple near Bundu whose foundation was laid in 1991 and consecrated in 1994 by the Sanskriti Vihar trust under Sita Ram Maroo. Shaped as a great chariot with eighteen wheels and seven horses and also housing Shiva, Parvati and Ganesha, it has become a leading Chhath Puja destination with bathing and pilgrim facilities.

name: Kalyaneshwari Temple
significance: A Shakta shrine near Asansol described as some five centuries old, with the present temple built by Gurudin Prasad Pal. It is best known as a place of pilgrimage for childless women seeking a boon from the goddess.
story: Legend holds that human sacrifices were once offered at Kalyaneshwari in the distant past.

name: Patali Srikhetra
significance: A pilgrimage site at the foot of Trikut Hill in Subarnapur district, revered as the place where the Jagannath images were hidden for safekeeping and drawing together Shakta, Buddhist and Vaishnava strands of worship. The hill also carries evidence of prehistoric settlement, giving the site archaeological as well as devotional weight.
story: The Madala Panji relates that King Sovanadeva concealed the images in the caves of Trikut Hill during Raktavahu's invasion, where they stayed 144 years until King Yayati Keshari recovered them.

name: Jagannath Temple, Delhi
significance: A Jagannath temple in the Safdarjung Development Area of Hauz Khas, built by Delhi's Odia community as its main religious centre in the capital. Its annual Rath Yatra procession draws thousands and is among the largest Odia cultural observances outside Odisha.

name: Malleswara Shiva Temple
significance: A laterite Shiva temple at Chandrakona, 26 feet square and about 60 feet tall, carrying five ridged rekha turrets over a triple-arched porch and finished in decorative stucco. Built in the Bhan period and renovated by Maharaja Tejchandra in 1831, it is a notable survival of 18th-century Bengal temple architecture.

name: Rani Sati Mandir, Mahuda
significance: A temple to Rani Sati Dadi in the Mahuda area of Dhanbad district, completed on 20 February 1992. It is a prominent local shrine whose calendar centres on the annual Varshika Puja and on the celebration of its founding day.

name: Vasudev Doul
significance: A Vaishnava temple of mud brick on a pancharatha plan, raised around 1680 under the patronage of the Ahom king Sulikphaa and counted among the better examples of late-medieval Ahom building. Protected by both the Assam government and the ASI, it remains the focus of local Doul Utsav and Bohag Bihu observances.
story: Local tradition says the temple once bore a golden finial that was carried off during invasions.
